claim: APEX-RIP combines peroxidase-catalyzed, spatially restricted in situ protein biotinylation with RNA-protein chemical crosslinking.
source: Here, we develop such a method, termed APEX-RIP, which combines peroxidase-catalyzed, spatially restricted in situ protein biotinylation with RNA-protein chemical crosslinking.
evidence: The abstract directly states the method combines these two techniques.

claim: APEX-RIP can isolate RNAs from the mitochondrial matrix using a single protocol.
source: We demonstrate that, using a single protocol, APEX-RIP can isolate RNAs from a variety of subcellular compartments, including the mitochondrial matrix, nucleus, cytosol, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER), with specificity and sensitivity that rival or exceed those of conventional approaches.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states APEX-RIP can isolate RNAs from the mitochondrial matrix.

claim: Spatial compartmentalization of RNA is central to many biological processes across all kingdoms of life.

evidence: The introduction makes a broad statement about the importance of RNA localization.

claim: APEX is an engineered peroxidase that can be targeted by genetic fusion to various subcellular regions of interest.
source: APEX is an engineered peroxidase that can be targeted by genetic fusion to various subcellular regions of interest (Rhee et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The results section describes APEX and cites a reference for its properties.

claim: Upon addition of biotin-phenol and hydrogen peroxide to live cells, APEX catalyzes the formation of biotin-phenoxyl radicals.
source: Upon addition of its substrates—biotin-phenol (BP) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)—to live cells, APEX catalyzes the formation of biotin-phenoxyl radicals that then diffuse outward and covalently biotinylate nearby endogenous proteins.
evidence: The results section describes the mechanism of APEX-catalyzed biotinylation.

claim: Biotin-phenoxyl radicals diffuse outward and covalently biotinylate nearby endogenous proteins.
source: Upon addition of its substrates—biotin-phenol (BP) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)—to live cells, APEX catalyzes the formation of biotin-phenoxyl radicals that then diffuse outward and covalently biotinylate nearby endogenous proteins.
evidence: The results section describes the mechanism of APEX-catalyzed biotinylation.

claim: The biotin-phenoxyl radical has a half-life of less than one millisecond.
source: More distal proteins are not significantly labeled because the biotin-phenoxyl radical has a half-life of less than one millisecond (Wishart and Madhava Rao, 2010).
evidence: The results section cites a reference for the half-life of the biotin-phenoxyl radical.

claim: APEX-catalyzed proximity biotinylation coupled to streptavidin enrichment and mass spectrometry can generate proteomic maps of the mitochondrial matrix with <5 nm spatial specificity.
source: Previous work has shown that APEX-catalyzed proximity biotinylation, coupled to streptavidin enrichment and mass spectrometry, can generate proteomic maps of the mitochondrial matrix, intermembrane space, outer membrane, and nucleoid, each with <5 nm spatial specificity (Rhee et al., 2013; Hung et al., 2014, 2017; Han et al., 2017).
evidence: The results section cites references for previous APEX proteomic mapping work.

claim: APEX-catalyzed proximity biotinylation coupled to streptavidin enrichment and mass spectrometry can generate proteomic maps of the mitochondrial intermembrane space with <5 nm spatial specificity.

evidence: The results section cites references for previous APEX proteomic mapping work.

evidence: The results section cites references for previous APEX proteomic mapping work.

claim: All 13 mitochondrially-encoded mRNAs were highly enriched by mito-APEX2-RIP.
source: Gene-level analysis comparing fold enrichment and statistical significance of all human genes (Materials and methods) revealed that all 13 mRNAs and both rRNAs encoded by the mitochondrial genome were highly enriched (greater than 11-fold; Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The results section describes RNA-Seq analysis showing enrichment of mitochondrial mRNAs, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Both mitochondrially-encoded rRNAs were highly enriched by mito-APEX2-RIP.
source: Gene-level analysis comparing fold enrichment and statistical significance of all human genes (Materials and methods) revealed that all 13 mRNAs and both rRNAs encoded by the mitochondrial genome were highly enriched (greater than 11-fold; Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The results section describes RNA-Seq analysis showing enrichment of mitochondrial rRNAs, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Several mitochondrial-encoded tRNAs were enriched by mito-APEX2-RIP.
source: Surprisingly, we even observed the enrichment of several mitochondrial-encoded tRNAs, although our library preparation workflow generally excluded such smaller RNA species (Figure 1D).
evidence: The results section describes unexpected enrichment of mitochondrial tRNAs, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: APEX-RIP enriched 5740 nuclear RNAs with observed contamination frequency of <1.6%.
source: We used Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis to obtain final transcript lists of 5740 nuclear RNAs and 5367 cytosolic RNAs, with observed contamination frequencies (i.e. the ratio of enriched off-target RNAs to total enriched RNAs) of <1.6% and <1.5%, respectively (Supplementary file 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The results section reports the number of nuclear RNAs enriched and their contamination frequency.

claim: APEX-RIP enriched 5367 cytosolic RNAs with observed contamination frequency of <1.5%.
source: We used Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis to obtain final transcript lists of 5740 nuclear RNAs and 5367 cytosolic RNAs, with observed contamination frequencies (i.e. the ratio of enriched off-target RNAs to total enriched RNAs) of <1.6% and <1.5%, respectively (Supplementary file 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The results section reports the number of cytosolic RNAs enriched and their contamination frequency.

claim: 3161 mRNAs appeared preferentially nuclear by APEX-RIP.
source: Surprisingly, we also observed sizeable populations of RNAs exhibiting noncanonical nuclear–cytoplasmic partitioning. 3161 mRNAs—including C1orf63, for example (Figure 2D, top right)—appeared preferentially nuclear.
evidence: The results section reports the number of mRNAs with nuclear localization, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: 81 lncRNAs appeared preferentially cytoplasmic by APEX-RIP.
source: Conversely, 81 lncRNAs appeared preferentially cytoplasmic (Figure 2D, bottom left); these include the known cytoplasmic lncRNA SNHG5, a modulator of staufen-mediated decay that influences colorectal tumor growth (Derrien et al., 2012; Damas et al., 2016) (Figure 2D, bottom right).
evidence: The results section reports the number of lncRNAs with cytoplasmic localization, with reference to Figure 2D and citations.

claim: SNHG5 is a known cytoplasmic lncRNA that is a modulator of staufen-mediated decay.
source: Conversely, 81 lncRNAs appeared preferentially cytoplasmic (Figure 2D, bottom left); these include the known cytoplasmic lncRNA SNHG5, a modulator of staufen-mediated decay that influences colorectal tumor growth (Derrien et al., 2012; Damas et al., 2016) (Figure 2D, bottom right).
evidence: The results section cites references describing SNHG5 function.

claim: SNHG5 influences colorectal tumor growth.
source: Conversely, 81 lncRNAs appeared preferentially cytoplasmic (Figure 2D, bottom left); these include the known cytoplasmic lncRNA SNHG5, a modulator of staufen-mediated decay that influences colorectal tumor growth (Derrien et al., 2012; Damas et al., 2016) (Figure 2D, bottom right).
evidence: The results section cites references describing SNHG5 function in cancer.

claim: 63% of nuclear RNAs enriched by fractionation-Seq were also enriched in the APEX-RIP nuclear dataset.
source: Of these RNAs, 63% (3358) were also enriched in our APEX-RIP nuclear dataset, implying general agreement between the two technologies (Figure 2E).
evidence: The results section compares APEX-RIP to fractionation-Seq, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: APEX-RIP nuclear dataset exhibited 1.6% ER contaminants.
source: Satisfyingly, each nuclear dataset exhibited similarly low levels of ER contaminants (1.6% and 1.3%, respectively, Figure 2F, left).
evidence: The results section reports contamination levels in APEX-RIP, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: Fractionation-Seq nuclear dataset exhibited 1.3% ER contaminants.
source: Satisfyingly, each nuclear dataset exhibited similarly low levels of ER contaminants (1.6% and 1.3%, respectively, Figure 2F, left).
evidence: The results section reports contamination levels in fractionation-Seq, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: 53.6% of annotated lncRNAs are enriched in the APEX-RIP-derived nuclear dataset.
source: Of these lncRNAs, 53.6% are enriched in our APEX-RIP-derived nuclear dataset, while nuclear Fractionation-Seq from the same cell line enriched only 42.2% (Figure 2F, right).
evidence: The results section compares lncRNA coverage between methods, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: 42.2% of annotated lncRNAs are enriched in the nuclear Fractionation-Seq dataset.
source: Of these lncRNAs, 53.6% are enriched in our APEX-RIP-derived nuclear dataset, while nuclear Fractionation-Seq from the same cell line enriched only 42.2% (Figure 2F, right).
evidence: The results section compares lncRNA coverage between methods, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: APEX-RIP rivals or outperforms Fractionation-Seq in terms of both specificity and coverage for analysis of endogenous RNA subcellular localization.
source: We conclude that APEX-RIP rivals or outperforms Fractionation-Seq in terms of both specificity and coverage, for analysis of endogenous RNA subcellular localization.
evidence: The results section makes a comparative conclusion about APEX-RIP performance.

claim: HRP-KDEL APEX-RIP efficiently enriched target secretome mRNAs relative to non-target controls with average fold enrichment of 19.5.
source: Intriguingly, while APEX-RIP from HRP-KDEL cells efficiently enriched target secretome mRNAs relative to non-target controls (average fold enrichment = 19.5, two-tailed t-test p-value = 0.00009), parallel experiments in ERM-APEX2 cells exhibited only modest, qualitative enrichment of target species (average fold enrichment = 1.49, two-tailed t-test p-value = 0.0515).
evidence: The results section reports quantitative enrichment data for HRP-KDEL.

claim: ERM-APEX2 APEX-RIP exhibited only modest enrichment of target species with average fold enrichment of 1.49.
source: Intriguingly, while APEX-RIP from HRP-KDEL cells efficiently enriched target secretome mRNAs relative to non-target controls (average fold enrichment = 19.5, two-tailed t-test p-value = 0.00009), parallel experiments in ERM-APEX2 cells exhibited only modest, qualitative enrichment of target species (average fold enrichment = 1.49, two-tailed t-test p-value = 0.0515).
evidence: The results section reports quantitative enrichment data for ERM-APEX2.

claim: APEX-RIP does not have the same spatial specificity as peroxidase-catalyzed proteomic labeling.
source: Our data strongly imply that APEX-RIP does not have the same spatial specificity as peroxidase-catalyzed proteomic labeling, and may be limited by perturbations induced by formaldehyde crosslinking.
evidence: The results section makes an inference about APEX-RIP spatial specificity based on experimental data.

claim: APEX-RIP may be limited by perturbations induced by formaldehyde crosslinking.
source: Our data strongly imply that APEX-RIP does not have the same spatial specificity as peroxidase-catalyzed proteomic labeling, and may be limited by perturbations induced by formaldehyde crosslinking.
evidence: The results section speculates about a limitation of APEX-RIP.

claim: 72% of secretome mRNAs expressed in HEK293T cells were enriched by HRP-KDEL APEX-RIP.
source: Gene-level analysis, comparing RNA counts before and after streptavidin pulldown, revealed that the majority (72%) of secretome mRNAs expressed in our cells (defined by ER-proximal RNAs (Jan et al., 2014) and Phobius-predicted mRNAs with exclusion of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs, see Materials and methods) were enriched, while mRNAs in a test set of known non-secreted genes were not enriched, thus demonstrating the ability of our method to isolate ER-associated transcripts from the larger population of cellular RNAs (Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section reports the percentage of secretome mRNAs enriched, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: APEX-RIP obtained a final list of 2672 ER-associated RNAs that were significantly enriched.
source: Using p-values and ROC analysis, we determined the optimal log2 fold change significance threshold (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F; see Materials and methods), obtaining a final list of 2672 ER-associated RNAs that were significantly enriched in multiple experiments (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: The results section reports the number of ER-associated RNAs identified, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The ER-associated RNA dataset exhibited 96.5% specificity based on secretory annotation.
source: However, this dataset exhibited 96.5% specificity, based on previous secretory annotation as defined by GOCC, SignalP, TMHMM, or Phobius (Ashburner et al., 2000; Petersen et al., 2011; Krogh et al., 2001; Käll et al., 2004), while mRNAs lacking such signals were concomitantly depleted (Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section reports specificity of ER dataset, with reference to Figure 4C and citations.

claim: The ER-associated RNA dataset exhibited 97% coverage as gauged by recall of 71 mRNAs encoding well-established ER resident proteins.
source: Coverage was likewise exceptional (97%), as gauged by the successful recall of 71 mRNAs encoding well-established ER resident proteins (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 3E; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The results section reports coverage of ER dataset, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: KDEL-APEX-RIP captures 69% of RNAs enriched by ER biochemical fractionation.
source: Encouragingly, KDEL-APEX-RIP captures the majority of RNAs enriched by each of these alternative techniques (69% and 97%, respectively, Figure 4E), implying broad agreement between the different methodologies.
evidence: The results section compares APEX-RIP to fractionation, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: KDEL-APEX-RIP captures 97% of RNAs enriched by proximity-dependent ribosome profiling.
source: Encouragingly, KDEL-APEX-RIP captures the majority of RNAs enriched by each of these alternative techniques (69% and 97%, respectively, Figure 4E), implying broad agreement between the different methodologies.
evidence: The results section compares APEX-RIP to ribosome profiling, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: APEX-RIP and ribosome profiling exhibited similarly high specificity (96.5% and 99.2%, respectively).
source: Specificity analysis demonstrated that APEX-RIP and ribosome profiling exhibited similarly high specificity (96.5% and 99.2%, respectively).
evidence: The results section compares specificity between methods.

claim: ER Fractionation-Seq exhibited 91% specificity such that only 91% of enriched mRNAs bore a secretory annotation.
source: However, Fractionation-Seq was substantially noisier, such that only 91% of enriched mRNAs bore a secretory annotation (Figure 4C); the remaining 9% comprised sizeable populations of conspicuous contaminants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The results section reports specificity of fractionation-Seq, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The coverage of ER-localized mRNAs retrieved by APEX-RIP (97%) was considerably higher than those retrieved by Fractionation-Seq (73%).
source: The coverage of ER-localized mRNAs retrieved by APEX-RIP (97%) was also considerably higher than those retrieved by both Fractionation-Seq and ribosome profiling (73% and 70%, respectively, Figure 4D).
evidence: The results section compares coverage between methods, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The coverage of ER-localized mRNAs retrieved by APEX-RIP (97%) was considerably higher than those retrieved by ribosome profiling (70%).
source: The coverage of ER-localized mRNAs retrieved by APEX-RIP (97%) was also considerably higher than those retrieved by both Fractionation-Seq and ribosome profiling (73% and 70%, respectively, Figure 4D).
evidence: The results section compares coverage between methods, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Of the 2494 mRNAs in the ER-associated RNA dataset, 135 code for mitochondrial proteins.
source: However, of the 2494 mRNAs in our ER-associated RNA dataset, 135 code for mitochondrial proteins, as defined by GOCC.
evidence: The results section reports the number of mitochondrial protein-coding mRNAs in the ER dataset.

claim: 132 of 135 mitochondrial protein-coding mRNAs in the ER dataset also carry secretory annotation.
source: Since the majority of these genes (132 mRNAs, 98%) also carry secretory annotation, we considered the possibility that the translation or processing of these 135 mRNAs require machinery localized at the ER membrane.
evidence: The results section reports the overlap between mitochondrial and secretory annotations.

claim: 62.7% of ER-proximal mitochondrial mRNAs code for transmembrane proteins.
source: Intriguingly, 62.7% of these mRNAs code for transmembrane proteins (as predicted by TMHMM), compared to only 20.4% of all nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section reports the percentage of transmembrane proteins, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: 20.4% of all nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes code for transmembrane proteins.
source: Intriguingly, 62.7% of these mRNAs code for transmembrane proteins (as predicted by TMHMM), compared to only 20.4% of all nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section reports the percentage of transmembrane proteins in the general mitochondrial proteome, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: 49% of ER-proximal mitochondrial genes with compartment-specific annotations encode proteins destined for the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: Subcompartment analysis of this ER-proximal population was also revealing: of the 39 genes for which compartment-specific annotations were available, 49% (19 genes) encode proteins destined for the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), whereas OMM proteins comprise only 18% of the bulk mitochondrial proteome (Figure 5B).
evidence: The results section reports subcompartment analysis, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: OMM proteins comprise only 18% of the bulk mitochondrial proteome.
source: Subcompartment analysis of this ER-proximal population was also revealing: of the 39 genes for which compartment-specific annotations were available, 49% (19 genes) encode proteins destined for the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM), whereas OMM proteins comprise only 18% of the bulk mitochondrial proteome (Figure 5B).
evidence: The results section reports the percentage of OMM proteins in the general mitochondrial proteome, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: 104 candidate laminar RNAs were identified by intersecting ER-associated and nuclear RNA lists.
source: When we performed this analysis, and filtered this intersected list to remove mRNAs that encode secretory proteins (for which our quantification may convolve nuclear-retained pre-mRNAs and mature ER-localized transcripts), we observed 104 candidate laminar RNAs, including 48 mRNAs and 56 noncoding RNA species (Figure 5D; Supplementary file 4B).
evidence: The results section reports the number of candidate laminar RNAs, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: The 104 candidate laminar RNAs include 48 mRNAs and 56 noncoding RNA species.
source: When we performed this analysis, and filtered this intersected list to remove mRNAs that encode secretory proteins (for which our quantification may convolve nuclear-retained pre-mRNAs and mature ER-localized transcripts), we observed 104 candidate laminar RNAs, including 48 mRNAs and 56 noncoding RNA species (Figure 5D; Supplementary file 4B).
evidence: The results section reports the composition of candidate laminar RNAs, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: APEX-RIP is simple, versatile, and does not require special instrumentation.
source: Since APEX-RIP is simple, versatile, and does not require special instrumentation, we envision its broad application in a variety of biological contexts.
evidence: The abstract makes claims about the practical advantages of APEX-RIP.

claim: APEX2 is a more active APEX variant than APEX.
source: We furthermore employed HEK293T cells that stably expressed mitochondrially-localized APEX2 (mito-APEX2, Figure 1B–C, Supplementary file 5A-B), a more active APEX variant that we hypothesized might improve target enrichment (Lam et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites a reference describing APEX2 as more active than APEX.

claim: HRP catalyzes the same proximity-dependent biotinylation chemistry as APEX2.
source: We have shown that HRP catalyzes the same proximity-dependent biotinylation chemistry as APEX2 (Loh et al., 2016), but has higher specific activity than APEX2 in the ER lumen (Lam et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites references describing HRP chemistry.

claim: HRP has higher specific activity than APEX2 in the ER lumen.
source: We have shown that HRP catalyzes the same proximity-dependent biotinylation chemistry as APEX2 (Loh et al., 2016), but has higher specific activity than APEX2 in the ER lumen (Lam et al., 2015).
evidence: The results section cites a reference describing HRP activity in the ER lumen.
